Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), as a class, have been associated with renal papillary necrosis and other abnormal renal pathologies when administered long-term in animal studies. 2. Another form of renal toxicity linked to NSAIDs is observed in patients with conditions that reduce renal blood flow or blood volume. In such cases, renal prostaglandins play a critical role in maintaining renal perfusion. 3. In these patients, the administration of an NSAID leads to a dose-dependent decrease in prostaglandin synthesis, which subsequently reduces renal blood flow. This reduction can result in overt renal decompensation. 4. Patients at the highest risk for this reaction include those with impaired renal function, heart failure, liver dysfunction, those taking diuretics, and elderly individuals. 5. Discontinuation of NSAID therapy typically results in recovery to the pretreatment state. 6. Similar to other NSAIDs, borderline elevations in one or more liver function tests may occur in up to 15% of patients taking nabumetone. 7. These liver test abnormalities may progress, remain unchanged, or return to normal with continued therapy. 8. The alanine aminotransferase (ALT, also known as SGPT) test is likely the most sensitive indicator of liver dysfunction. 9. Significant elevations (three times the upper limit of normal) in ALT (SGPT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST, also known as SGOT) have been observed in controlled clinical trials of nabumetone (Relafen) in less than 1% of patients. 10. Patients presenting with symptoms or signs suggestive of liver dysfunction, or those with abnormal liver test results, should be evaluated for evidence of more severe hepatic reactions while on nabumetone therapy. 11. Severe hepatic reactions, including jaundice and fatal hepatitis, have been reported with nabumetone and other NSAIDs. 12. If a patient develops signs or symptoms of liver dysfunction (e.g., jaundice, rash, eosinophilia) while taking nabumetone, the drug should be discontinued immediately. 13. Nabumetone may be associated with an increased likelihood of photosensitivity reactions to sun exposure, beyond what might be expected based on skin tanning types.
